questions.question: Which type of mountains In the northwest, north and northeast bind India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Young fold mountains.**__

__** [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] Key Points__**

__
 
• **India is bounded by the Himalayas in the northwest, north and northeast.**
 
• The **Himalayas **are known as **young fold mountains** because they started to form in the Late Cretaceous to Tertiary era and are still rising in elevation.
 
• Due to the compressive forces created when the Asian and Indian/Australian continental plates collided, these mountains are known as fold mountains.
 
• Sedimentary rocks make up the Himalayan region.
 
• The average height of mountain peaks in the Himalayan region is about 6000 meters.
 
• It is the longest and most northern range and it is made up of snow glaciers and is coated in snow.
 
• It is made of granite and is symmetrical by nature and it has imposing mountains like Nanda Devi and Kanchenjunga.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Block mountains: **

 
 
• Block Mountains formed as the result of faulting caused by tensile and compressive forces motored by endogenetic forces coming from within the earth, also known as fault-block mountains.
 
• Block mountains repre­sent the upstanding parts of the ground between two faults or on either side of a rift valley or a graben.
 
 
 
• **Dome mountains:**
 
 
• Dome mountains are formed where a region of flat-lying sedimentary rocks is warped or bowed upward making a structural dome.
 
• Their topography is characterized by a relatively flat, dissected surface sloping gradually toward the surrounding lowlands, or basins.
 
• The diameters of the bases of dome mountains range up to hundreds of kilometres.
 
 
 
• **Plateau mountains:**
 
 
• Plateau mountains occur in series when the folds of a mountain chain pass abruptly into the horizontal strata of a basalt plateau that is largely denuded of trees and eroded.

questions.question: Which of the following water bodies are also known as nurseries of the ocean?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Estuaries**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Estuaries** are transition zones where freshwater from rivers meets and mixes with saltwater from the ocean, creating a unique ecological environment.
 
• They are often referred to as **"nurseries of the ocean"** because they provide critical breeding and feeding grounds for many marine species.
 
• Estuaries support a rich biodiversity, including fish, crustaceans, mollusks, and migratory birds, which thrive in their nutrient-rich waters.
 
• These areas are particularly important for the early life stages of commercially important fish species, such as salmon and shrimp.
 
• Estuaries play a vital role in maintaining water quality by filtering pollutants and sediments through their complex ecosystems.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Definition of Estuaries:**

 
 
• An estuary is a partially enclosed coastal body of water where freshwater from rivers and streams merges with saltwater from the sea.
 
• They typically have a dynamic salinity gradient, influenced by tides, river flow, and seasonal changes.
 
 
 
• **Importance of Estuaries:**
 
 
• Estuaries act as natural buffers, protecting coastlines from erosion and flooding.
 
• They are crucial for nutrient cycling and support primary productivity, forming the foundation of aquatic food webs.
 
 
 
• **Threats to Estuaries:**
 
 
• Human activities such as pollution, overfishing, and land reclamation pose significant threats to estuarine ecosystems.
 
• Climate change impacts, including rising sea levels and altered precipitation patterns, further endanger these vital habitats.
 
 
 
• **Difference Between Estuaries and Lagoons:**
 
 
• While estuaries are transition zones mixing freshwater and saltwater, lagoons are shallow coastal water bodies separated from the ocean by sandbars or barrier islands.
 
• Lagoons typically have less biodiversity compared to estuaries due to limited nutrient mixing.

• **Karst **is a distinctive topography in which the landscape is largely shaped by the dissolving action of water on **carbonate bedrock** such as **limestone and dolomite**, etc.

 
 
• When the rain falls through the atmosphere, it picks carbon dioxide which dissolves in the droplets.
 
• Once the rain hits the ground, it percolates through the soil and picks more carbon dioxide to form a weak solution of carbonic acid.
 
• The infiltrating water naturally exploits cracks in the rock.
 
• Over long periods, carbon bedrock begins to dissolve.
 
• Opening in bedrock increases in size and an underground drainage system begins to develop and allows more water to pass which further accelerates the formation process of karst.
 
• **Some of the landforms develop within the bedrock such as pools, sinkholes, doline, stalactites, stalagmites etc.**
